original_question: For each unpredictably emergent Costas-array construction method obtained by adding one or more dots to an existing Costas array, determine whether there is a finite threshold N beyond which that method never produces a Costas array of order n > N.
target_in_paper: Problem 11 in Section 5.2, 'Scope of dot addition methods'.
correct_elements: The draft correctly identifies the relevant class of constructions as the unpredictably emergent, dot-addition-type methods, asks the question method-by-method, and captures the paper's main quantitative issue: whether each such method eventually stops producing Costas arrays beyond some finite order threshold.
missing_details: The exact target is Problem 11, which asks first to determine the overall scope of the unpredictably emergent construction techniques discussed in Section 3.2, and only then singles out the threshold question as a particular formulation.

In the paper, 'unpredictably emergent' is a defined term: these are families obtained by transforming generated Costas arrays, whose Costas property cannot be guaranteed by any known condition other than direct verification.
The relevant methods are specifically the five heuristics of Section 3.2.2, not arbitrary future or ad hoc dot-addition procedures.
The starting arrays are the paper's algebraically generated Welch/Golomb Costas arrays over finite fields F(p) or F(p^m), not arbitrary pre-existing Costas arrays.
Some of the methods do more than simply add a dot to a finished array: the Rickard-type constructions first add blank row/column space and apply cyclic shifts, and then add a dot.
The threshold N is method-dependent and belongs to N; the quantifier is: for each method, there exists N such that no output of that method is a Costas array of order n > N.
The 'one or more dots' language is slightly too loose relative to the paper: among the five heuristics, one adds two anti-diametrical corner dots, while the others are one-dot transformations.
The paper motivates the question with explicit computational evidence in low and higher orders; this empirical context is implicit in the draft but part of the intended scope discussion.
refined_question: For each of the five unpredictably emergent Costas-array construction heuristics in Section 3.2.2—obtained by prescribed transformations of algebraically generated Welch/Golomb Costas arrays and whose outputs must be checked for the Costas property by direct verification—determine the scope of the method. In particular, for each such heuristic, does there exist a method-dependent integer N such that the heuristic produces no Costas arrays of order n > N?
justification: The draft is essentially a close paraphrase of the second sentence of Problem 11. The section title and the paragraph immediately before Problem 11 show that the paper is not asking about arbitrary extension procedures, but specifically about the unpredictably emergent 'dot addition' constructions introduced earlier. Definition 5 supplies the paper's technical meaning of 'unpredictably emergent', and Heuristics 1-5 specify exactly which methods are under discussion. I therefore sharpened the draft by tying it to those five Section 3.2.2 heuristics, restricting the source arrays to the paper's generated Welch/Golomb families, and making explicit that the cutoff N is allowed to depend on the method. I did not broaden the question to sporadic arrays or to alternative construction techniques, which are treated separately elsewhere in the paper.
